title: Free providers and agents
text:
This page lists the free ways to run the course exercises: the agents you type commands into, and the providers that supply the model behind them. Read Standard setup first for the base installation.
Written for: learners choosing their first agent, and volunteers who need to explain the options.

title: Free providers and agents
section: 2. The two layers: agent and model
text:
2. The two layers: agent and model
Every option has two parts, and it helps to keep them separate in your head:

The agent is the program you run. It reads your files, proposes edits and runs commands. Examples: Gemini CLI, Aider, Cline, OpenCode.
The model is the AI that does the thinking. It is supplied by a provider, such as Google, OpenRouter or a model running on your own computer.

Some agents only work with one provider (Gemini CLI works with Google). Others accept many providers (Aider, Cline and OpenCode accept OpenRouter and most others). Using an agent that accepts many providers gives you the most options if one provider runs out of free quota.

title: Free providers and agents
text:
3. The agents

Gemini CLI (Google)
A terminal agent from Google. It is the default for the course exercises.



Runs in
Terminal


Install
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli (needs Node.js, see Standard setup)


Sign-in
Your Google account, the first time you run gemini


Free limit (Google login, reported)
About 1,000 model requests per day and 60 per minute


Free limit (unpaid API key, reported)
About 250 requests per day and 10 per minute, Flash models only


Best for
Learners who want the fewest steps and no API key


Watch out for
The free tier and product name may change. Some reports say Gemini CLI is moving to Antigravity CLI. Check the official site before you rely on it.



Start it from your project folder with gemini. The first run asks you to sign in.


Aider (open source)
A terminal agent that works with almost any model. It edits your files directly and can commit each change to Git.







Runs in
Terminal


Install (official route)
python -m pip install aider-install, then run aider-install


Install (uv route)
uv tool install aider-chat


Key
An OpenRouter key, or a Google key, set as an environment variable


Best for
Learners who want to see every change and control the model directly


Watch out for
You choose the model yourself. Model names must be written exactly, for example openrouter/<provider>/<model>.



To use a free OpenRouter model, put the key in .env, then run:
aider --model openrouter/qwen/qwen3-coder:free
To see what is available, run aider --list-models openrouter/.


Cline (VS Code)
A free extension for VS Code with a visual panel. You bring your own key and pay the model provider, which can be zero on a free tier.







Runs in
VS Code


Install
VS Code Extensions panel, then search “Cline”


Key
OpenRouter key entered in Cline’s settings


Best for
Learners who are not yet comfortable in the terminal (Builder track)


Watch out for
The extension is free, but the model is not. Check the price of each model. Set a spending limit on your key.



In Cline’s settings, pick OpenRouter as the provider and paste your key. For free models, search the dropdown for “free”, or choose openrouter/free, which picks a free model for each request.


Continue (VS Code)
An open-source VS Code extension that works like Cline and accepts many providers. It is useful if you want a second option that runs inside the editor. Setup is similar to Cline: pick a provider and paste the key.


OpenCode (open source)
An open-source terminal agent that connects to many providers, including local models through Ollama. Sources report that it includes free models that work without an account, though the list rotates.



Runs in
Terminal


Install
brew install opencode (macOS or Linux with Homebrew), or npm install -g opencode-ai


Windows
Use WSL, as in Standard setup


Start
Go to your project folder and run opencode


Key
Optional for built-in free models; needed for OpenRouter or Google


Best for
Learners who want an open-source agent and may later use local models


Watch out for
Free models change without notice. Check the official docs (opencode.ai) for the current list.

title: Free providers and agents
text:
4. The providers

Google Gemini
Two ways to get free Gemini access:

Google login through Gemini CLI. No key needed. This is the simplest route and what the course default uses.
An API key from Google AI Studio. Free, no card required for the basic tier. Use it with Aider, Cline, OpenCode or any agent that accepts a Google key. Store it in .env as shown in Standard setup.

Free limits are per day and per minute, and they change. The unpaid API key allows far fewer requests than the Google login route.


OpenRouter
OpenRouter gives one account and one key for many models. Free models have IDs ending in :free.



Sign-up
https://openrouter.ai, create a key at the Keys page


Card
Not needed for free models


Limits (reported)
20 requests per minute. Daily limit is reported as 50 requests on the unfunded tier, and some sources say 200. Buying about USD 10 in credits raises the daily limit to 1,000. Check the current figure on openrouter.ai.


Model list
Changes often. Free models can be busy at peak hours and disappear without notice.


Data
Whether prompts are kept or used for training depends on the provider serving each model. Check the model’s page before sending anything sensitive.



Good first models to try are the ones marked :free on the model page. Some agents let you list fallback models, so that if one is busy another answers.


Local models (Ollama)
For private work, run a small model on your own computer. Nothing leaves your machine, but results are weaker and slower than hosted models. Use it for sensitive exercises only after a short test. Install Ollama from https://ollama.com, pull a small coding model, and point Aider, Cline or OpenCode at the local endpoint. Most learners with 8–16 GB RAM can run a model of about 1.5–8 billion parameters.

title: Development Paradigms - Theoretical and Practical
text:
📅 Date & Time: November 7, 2026 at 09:00 (9:00 AM UTC)
👨‍🏫 Presenter: Akshi Rao
🎯 Session Type: Comprehensive Theory + Hands-On Application (4-hour session with breaks)



This session bridges the gap between understanding Vibe Coding concepts and implementing them in production-level applications. Participants learn that “Vibe Coding” isn’t just about typing prompts—it requires understanding system design principles, business requirements, and software development lifecycle before engaging AI as a tool. The session emphasizes that system design is a founding principle of responsible AI development.





System Design First - Understand why proper planning prevents AI hallucination and wasted tokens
Spec-Driven Workflow - Learn the five-component system specification framework
Production-Level Coding - Build applications ready for real-world use, not just demos
Avoid Blind AI Trust - Understand limitations and when to stop prompting
End-to-End Deployment - From concept to hosted application







Historical Context: - Google and Amazon interviews require mastery of system design for software engineers - System design addresses: scalability, reliability, performance, security, maintainability - Building Facebook or Amazon requires complex system architecture across multiple data centers - Traditional development: Months or years to launch a production system
Current Vibe Coding Challenge: - People often launch applications without proper system design thinking - Result: Applications that work initially but fail under scale, security, or complexity - AI makes it easy to build something—but easy ≠ production-ready - Without system design, you waste tokens and create technical debt
The Principle: > Don’t just say “build a dashboard.” Say “build a scalable, secure dashboard with these specific requirements, this architecture, and these constraints.”



Anti-Pattern: Vague Requests
❌ "Build a dashboard"
❌ "Create a website"
❌ "Make a chatbot"
Why This Fails: - AI must guess what you want (token waste, hallucination) - Result likely doesn’t match your actual needs - May have security or architectural problems - You burn tokens before getting something usable
Better Pattern: Structured Specification
✅ Functional requirements clearly listed
✅ Non-functional requirements defined
✅ Interface design described
✅ Acceptance criteria specified
✅ Constraints and limitations noted



Every system should be defined by:



Definition: What MUST the system do?
Question: What is the core purpose and capability?
Example (Job Search App):

Search across 3 job websites
Filter by city and job title
Display results matching user skills






Definition: What qualities must it have? (Not “what does it do” but “how well does it do it?”)
Examples:

Performance: Response time < 2 seconds
Security: Comply with OWASP Top 10
Usability: Mobile-responsive, intuitive UI
Reliability: 99.9% uptime
Scalability: Handle 10,000 concurrent users






Definition: What are the LIMITS and RESTRICTIONS?
Examples:

“No hardcoded credentials”
“No external LLM API calls (cost control)”
“No complex authentication for MVP”
“HTML/CSS/JavaScript only”
“Deployable offline”






Definition: How do users interact with it?
Examples:

Design language (colors, typography)
Layout structure (one-page vs. multi-page)
Interaction patterns (scroll vs. click)
Accessibility requirements
Responsiveness targets (mobile-first? tablet-optimized?)






Definition: How do we measure SUCCESS?
Rule: Must be testable and measurable
Examples:

“Job matching accuracy: ≥ 90% based on keyword matching”
“Load time: < 1.5 seconds”
“No security warnings from Bandit/TruffleHog”
“All features documented and tested”






Example: Photo Sharing App (Like Instagram)
Brainstorming Round (What Matters?): - Authentication: How do users log in? Security level needed? - Security: Is this public? Data privacy requirements? GDPR/compliance? - Scroll Design: Is it infinitely scrolling (mobile) or paginated (desktop)? - UI/UX: What makes it “addictive” (intentional design)? - Functional Requirements: Upload, download, share, comment, like? - Non-Functional Requirements: Handle 1M users? Global scalability? Real-time notifications? - Back-end Storage: Need database? Cloud? CDN for images? - Performance: How fast must image loading be?
This exercise prevents: Building something cool but impractical



Traditional software development follows this flow:
Business Analyst (BA)  →  Developer  →  QA Tester  →  Production
    ↓                        ↓              ↓
Define Requirements     Implement       Verify Quality
What to build?          How to build?   Does it work?
                                        Is it secure?
The Vibe Coding Risk: - Many people skip from “What to build?” directly to “Build it with AI” - Bypassing design, testing, and security reviews - Result: Features that don’t match business needs, security vulnerabilities, poor user experience
Recommended Vibe Coding Process: 1. Business Requirements - Define spec using five components 2. AI Development - Generate code based on spec 3. Testing & Review - Verify code quality, security, functionality 4. QA Sign-off - Confirm acceptance criteria met 5. Production Deployment - Release with confidence



User Need: Daily curated job listings matching my CV and skills
Specification Using Five Components:
# Job Search Application Specification

## Functional Requirements
1. Search job listings across multiple job boards
2. Filter by: location (cities), job title, experience level
3. Store user preferences and CV information
4. Provide daily curated matches
5. Display job card with: title, company, salary, link

## Non-Functional Requirements
1. Load within 2 seconds
2. Mobile-responsive design (primary mobile use)
3. No authentication required for MVP
4. Scroll-based infinite or pagination-based interface
5. Pink color scheme with modern aesthetics

## Constraints
1. No LLM integration (cost control)
2. No complex backend; static deployment possible
3. No hardcoded credentials
4. No paid APIs (use free tier only)
5. Keyword matching only (no ML/complex algorithm initially)

## Interface Description
- Single-page application (one-page read-only view)
- Scroll through job cards
- One-click apply buttons
- Search filters at top
- Responsive to mobile screen sizes

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Successfully displays 10+ jobs per search
2. Filtering works correctly (location, title, experience)
3. Job matches meet 90% accuracy vs. user CV skills
4. No security warnings from Bandit/TruffleHog/Synk
5. Deployment successful on free tier (Render/Netlify)
6. Mobile loads within 2 seconds



Three Critical Decisions Before Prompting:

Which AI Tool? (Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, Gemini)
Which Model? (Claude Opus/Sonnet, GPT-4/3.5, Gemini Pro/Flash)
Which Mode? (Auto, Plan, Manual)

Recommended Approach: Plan Mode - Shows AI’s approach before executing - Allows review of architecture decisions - Reduces token waste from wrong approaches - Enables course-correction early
Prompt to AI (in Markdown):
# Job Search Application

## Functional Requirements
- Search across 3 websites (Indeed, LinkedIn, FlexJobs)
- Filter by: 3 cities, job titles A/B/C
- Simple search engine, no API needed
- Display results in responsive layout

## Non-Functional Requirements
- Load time < 2 seconds
- Mobile-first responsive design
- Pink and purple color scheme
- Accessible to non-technical users

## Constraints
- No LLM integration
- No authentication/OAuth
- Simple keyword matching only
- Deployable as static site

## Interface
- Single page, scroll design
- HTML/CSS/JavaScript only
- Job cards with apply buttons

## Acceptance Criteria
- 90% keyword match accuracy
- All jobs from latest daily refresh
- No security vulnerabilities
- Mobile load time < 1.5 seconds
- Successfully deployed to Render/Netlify
Key Advantage: This specification makes AI’s job much easier and more accurate



Step 1: Generate with Claude Code - AI creates initial artifact (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) - Download as ZIP file
Step 2: Open in VS Code - Extract ZIP in local directory - Open with VS Code - Integrate Claude Code extension in “Manual” mode
Step 3: Customize Offline - Change colors in CSS - Modify fonts and styling - Update copy/text - All without burning tokens
Step 4: Test Locally - Run Python: python3 -m http.server 8080 - Test in browser at localhost:8080 - Verify all features work
Step 5: Push to GitHub - git init in project folder - git add . - git commit -m "Initial job search app" - Create repo on GitHub - git remote add origin <repo-url> - git push -u origin main
Step 6: Deploy to Render/Netlify - Connect GitHub repo - Select branch (usually main) - Deploy (automatic on each push) - Get public URL
Step 7: Share & Monitor - Test deployed version on mobile/desktop - Share portfolio URL with employers - Monitor for any issues











Mistake
Impact
Prevention




No spec before prompting
Wasted tokens, wrong features
Write five-component spec first


Trusting AI blindly
Security issues, bugs
Always review, test, scan


Using only 1 AI model
Limited perspective
Have 2nd AI audit the code


Hardcoding secrets
Credential theft
Use .env files, never commit


Deploying without testing
Public-facing bugs
Always test locally first


Ignoring security warnings
Vulnerabilities in production
Run Bandit/TruffleHog/Synk


Over-engineering MVP
Wasted time, high cost
Simplify, iterate later


Assuming free tier === forever
Sudden cost increase
Plan upgrade path early






Decision Framework:
If AI Output = What You Want  →  Use It
If AI is Looping (same answer 3x)  →  Stop, Debug Manually
If AI Hallucinating Heavily  →  Provide More Context
If Simple Problem  →  Maybe just code it yourself
If Your Cost > Outcome Value  →  Manual is faster/cheaper
If Security-Critical  →  Always verify, never trust completely








Traditional Development: $100k+ salary × 1 engineer × 6 months = Expensive
Vibe Coding: $20/month subscription × 1 person × 1 month = Cheap
The Catch: Only works if you:

Know what you want (good spec)
Can verify it’s correct (technical understanding)
Can secure it (security review)
Can deploy it (DevOps knowledge)
Can maintain it (ongoing support)


Therefore: Vibe Coding is not a replacement for software engineering—it’s an accelerant for people who understand software engineering.






Define Your Problem: Choose an application you want to build
Write Five-Component Spec: Don’t skip this step
Prompt Claude Code: Use the spec as your prompt
Test Locally: Verify all features work on your machine
Run Security Scans: Bandit, TruffleHog, Synk
Deploy to Free Tier: Get it on the internet
Share and Iterate: Get feedback, improve





Personal Portfolio/Job Search App Build: - Use this exact framework - Share your deployed URL - Cohort can provide feedback - Builds portfolio for interviews/job applications





“The biggest drawback of Vibe-based coding is failing to scale. Start with the basics and always remember: speed is now available to everyone. Your advantage is ensuring fast code is also safe, strong, and professional.”

The mindset shift: - Old: “Can I code this?” → New: “Should I build this? And how do I verify it’s right?” - From code writer → to system architect and quality gate





OWASP Top 10: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/
System Design Interview Prep: Books like “System Design Interview” by Alex Xu
Render.com Deployment: https://render.com/docs
Netlify Deployment: https://docs.netlify.com/
GitHub Basics: https://docs.github.com/en


💡 Instructor Note: This session emphasizes that Vibe Coding is not a shortcut around software engineering—it’s a tool for those who understand software engineering to move faster.

A: Multiple approaches: 1. Run security scanners (Bandit, TruffleHog, Synk) 2. Have second AI agent review code 3. Use deterministic tools for sensitive operations 4. Test in safe environments before production 5. Keep humans in charge of critical operations

A: Yes! Perfect approach: - Model A writes the code - Model B from different vendor audits the code - Model A fixes issues - Result: Much higher quality

A: Yes, but different: - Speed: 100x faster (minutes vs. months) - Cost: 1000x cheaper ($ vs. $k) - Catch: Requires human judgment to verify - Trade: You become the architect/reviewer, not code writer

AI models are trained primarily on content from GitHub, Stack Overflow, and technical documentation—all written in Markdown format. This makes Markdown the “native language” of AI.
Best Practices: - Hash signs (#) = Mark important sections - Code blocks (```) = Clearly show code boundaries - Bullet points = Show order and priority - Together = Reduces hallucination significantly

# Login System Requirements
## Functional Requirements
- User registration with email validation
- Secure password storage (bcrypt)
- Session management with JWT tokens

## Constraints
- NO passwords in code
- NO hardcoded credentials
- MUST follow OWASP standards



Every word sent to AI incurs costs measured in “tokens.”
Three Money-Saving Tips: 1. Use System Prompts - Put fixed rules at the top (can be 10x cheaper when reused) 2. Send Only What’s Needed - Don’t send entire projects to fix one function 3. Model Selection - Use smaller models for easy tasks; reserve big models for complex work (design, security)

title: Session VI: Agents Mechanisms
text:
What we covered

Five levels of AI:

Naked LLM: text in, text out.
Augmented LLM: the model can use a few tools, such as search or files.
Workflow: several steps run in a fixed order.
Agent: the model decides its own next steps.
Multi-agent: a team of specialised agents works on the same goal.

Use the simplest level that works. Translating a paragraph needs only an LLM. Booking a room with a fallback option needs an agent.
The agentic loop: Plan, act (use a tool), observe the result, and repeat until the goal is met.
Tools: A calculator, web search, code execution, file access, a browser or email. Tools let the AI get exact answers instead of guessing.
Memory: Short-term memory is the conversation. Long-term memory is in project files, such as a memory.md.
Four planning patterns: Think step by step, react (reason, then act), plan-execute with a to-do list, and check and fix.
Cost: Every loop costs tokens, so agents are expensive for simple or high-volume tasks.

title: Session VI: Agents Mechanisms
text:
Key takeaway

An agent is not better than an LLM. It is more complex and more expensive. Use an agent only when the task needs adaptive decisions.

title: Session VIII: Multi-Agents Orchestration
text:
What we covered

Why now: The presenter cited figures for 2025: about 80% of the code companies ship is AI-generated, and about 27% of AI-generated code contains security vulnerabilities.
From Software 1.0 to natural language: Coding moved from hand-written programs, to trained models, to describing what you want in plain English.
AI-first development: Agents can take part in each stage of the lifecycle, from requirements to operations. People stay in charge of direction and governance.
The Four D Framework:

Delegation: Decide what to hand to AI, and how much control it gets (automation, augmentation or agency).
Description: Describe the goal and the constraints precisely.
Discernment: Check the output for accuracy, alignment, sound reasoning and whether it solves your real problem.
Diligence: Use AI ethically and transparently, and take responsibility for the results.

Building blocks: Models, then agents (a model with tools, memory and a loop), then teams (agents that send messages and share artifacts).
A coordinated team: A coordinator hands work to specialist agents, which run in parallel. A validator checks the results, a writer produces the output, and a human reviews and decides.
ChatDev: A team of agents with different roles builds software through a chat chain. Agents ask clarifying questions before answering, which reduces hallucinations.
MetaGPT: Agents follow human-style procedures and play familiar roles: product manager, architect, engineer, QA engineer and project manager.
Limits today: Agents handle simple logic and prototypes well, but production systems need more. They can use unsafe defaults such as static credentials, and they use more tokens than a single agent. Use multiple agents when the task needs several kinds of expertise or quality checks.
Your role: The presenter’s analogy is a head chef, who designs the kitchen, coordinates the staff and owns every dish.
Homework: Read the ChatDev and MetaGPT papers, and think about a task that could use a team of agents.

title: Session VIII: Multi-Agents Orchestration
text:
Key takeaway

Vibe coding alone is not engineering. Vibe coding with supervision is. Multi-agent orchestration is how we build safely and sustainably, and you are the architect, quality gate and governance authority.

Three primary open-source tools for detecting vulnerabilities in AI-generated code:



Purpose: Scans Python code for security issues
Detection: SQL injection, path traversal, dangerous functions
Example Finding: Hardcoded passwords, weak cryptography
Limitation: Python-only; Semgrep is language-agnostic alternative
Usage: bandit <filename.py> or bandit -r . (recursive)





Purpose: Detects hardcoded credentials in source code
Detection: API keys, tokens, passwords embedded in code
Why Critical: Exposed credentials on public GitHub = instant compromise
Cost Impact: One leaked API key can drain your budget rapidly if used by malicious actors
Usage: Direct scan from CLI or via their website





Purpose: Checks installed libraries for known vulnerabilities
Why Important: Third-party dependencies often contain outdated/vulnerable versions
Process: Scans requirements.txt or similar dependency files
Output: Shows which packages are outdated and have security vulnerabilities
Action: Update vulnerable libraries or consult documentation for patches





Before building anything, establish five key specifications:


1. Functional Requirements
   - What MUST the system do?
   - Core features and operations
   - Example: "Search job listings across 3 websites for specific cities and roles"

2. Non-Functional Requirements
   - What else does it need? (Performance, security, usability)
   - Example: "Security compliant with OWASP Top 10", "Load under 2 seconds"
   - Example: "Scroll-worthy design, one-page read-only interface"

3. Constraints
   - What are the LIMITS?
   - Example: "No hardcoded credentials", "No LLM integration required"
   - Example: "HTML/CSS/JavaScript only"

4. Interface Description
   - How does the user interact?
   - Visual design, layout, interaction patterns
   - Example: "Pink color scheme with dark mode support"

5. Acceptance Criteria
   - How do we know it's DONE?
   - Measurable success metrics
   - Example: "Job matches must be 90% accurate based on keyword matching"




Project Brief: - Goal: Create a web application that searches job listings and matches them to user CV - Users: Job seekers (non-technical to semi-technical) - Key Feature: Curated, relevant job suggestions delivered daily
System Design Decisions: - Frontend: HTML/CSS/JavaScript (no complex backend initially) - Data Source: Web scraping + simple keyword matching - Database: Simple local storage initially (optional backend upgrade) - Security: No authentication/OAuth required for MVP - Cost: Minimize API calls; use free tier services where possible

🎯 Session Type: Theoretical Framework + Research Paper Analysis

This session fundamentally shifts perspective from individual agents to coordinated multi-agent systems. Lwin introduces why multi-agent orchestration is not a future concept but an urgent present-day necessity. The session covers the Four D Framework (Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence), architectural foundations, and analysis of two seminal research papers (ChatDev and MetaGPT) that demonstrate multi-agent collaboration in action.





Understand Multi-Agent Necessity - Know why single agents are insufficient for complex tasks

Analyze Real Research - Learn from ChatDev and MetaGPT approaches

Recognize Governance Shift - Understand your new role in human-in-the-loop orchestration









Reason 1: The Shift is Already Here - As of December 2025: 80% of code that companies ship is AI-generated - This is not theoretical; this is production reality today - The window to learn how to do this safely is NOW
Reason 2: Security Vulnerabilities in AI Code - As of 2025: 27.4% of AI-generated code contains security vulnerabilities - Example vulnerabilities: - Hardcoded credentials and API keys - SQL injection vulnerabilities - Weak cryptography implementations - Missing authentication/authorization - This is not a future risk; it’s a current incident rate
Reason 3: The Competitive Imperative - Companies shipping flawed AI code will compound problems - This training equips you to use AI safely and effectively - Without this knowledge: You’ll ship bugs and vulnerabilities - With this knowledge: You’ll build robust, secure systems
Key Insight: Every developer must learn this NOW, regardless of technical background








Who: Professional developers only (rare, expensive skill)
How: Write explicit instructions in programming languages (Python, Java, C++, PHP)
Knowledge Required: Deep programming paradigm expertise

Access: Limited to specialists

Who: Anyone who can describe what they want (democratized)

Access: Universal; no coding experience required

The Fundamental Shift: > “The hottest new programming language is English” — Andrej Karpathy, Founder of OpenAI
Key Insight from Research: - Andrej Karpathy coined this in February 2025 - Named “Coding” as World of the Year 2025 - This validates that natural language IS the new programming interface
New Skills That Matter: 1. Knowing what to build (requirements) 2. Knowing why (business context) 3. Knowing how to verify (quality assurance) 4. Knowing how to coordinate (multi-agent orchestration)

❌ "Build a chatbot"

Key Practice: The more precise your description, the better the AI output



Question: How do I know the AI output is correct?
Four Quality Checks:

Accuracy: Is the output correct and error-free?
Alignment: Did the AI follow my instructions?
Reasoning: Did the AI use sound logic?
Goal Alignment: Does this solve my actual problem?

Golden Rule: > “Never publish what you haven’t personally read and verified. You are accountable.”
Cost of Poor Discernment: - 27.4% of AI code has vulnerabilities - Security breaches from shipped bugs - Reputational damage - Legal liability



Question: Am I using AI responsibly?

Is this AI appropriate for this context?

Explain limitations to stakeholders

Am I accountable for the output?

You own the results, even if AI created them
You must verify correctness
You bear responsibility for failures

Lwin provides precise definitions for essential concepts:


Artificial Intelligence: Systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence - Examples: Speech recognition, image interpretation, language translation, recommendations

Decision Making: Choose among alternatives using evidence, constraints, and understanding who has authority
Problem Solving: Find gap between current and desired state, break into steps, try solutions, verify results

AI Agent: Uses AI model to interpret context, choose actions, use available tools to pursue goals, adjust based on results
Multi-Agent System: Multiple agents interact and coordinate work. Coordination can be supervised or distributed.
Flocking (Emergent behavior): Coordinated group movement from local rules - Separation: Avoid crowding - Alignment: Follow neighbors’ heading - Cohesion: Steer toward average position

Lwin analyzes the first seminal research paper: ChatDev


A chat-powered software development framework that uses multiple LLM-driven agents with different roles to build software through multi-agent collaboration.
Key Innovation: Uses chat chain (structured communication) + communicative de-hallucination (asking for clarification before responding)



Design Phase → Coding Phase → Testing Phase

Solution: Before responding, agents ask clarifying questions: - “What exactly do you need?” - “Can you provide more detail?” - “Should I interpret this as X or Y?”
Result: Significantly reduces hallucinations



Two Types of Memory:

Short-term Memory: Maintains dialogue continuity within a single phase
Long-term Memory: Preserves context across different phases

Problem Addressed: LLM context windows are limited (can’t remember everything) Solution: Segment memory based on phase



Key Findings: - Multi-agent collaboration produces more coherent solutions - Role assignment significantly impacts quality - Without role specification: Output is generic - With role specification: Output is targeted - De-hallucination mechanism reduces errors across all metrics - Communication patterns are critical to quality

Limitation 4: Computational Cost - Multi-agents require MORE tokens than single agents - More time, more computation, higher environmental impact - Optimization needed to reduce interactions

Definition: LLM with access to 1-3 tools (search, files, memory)
Capability: Can access external information or perform limited actions
Limitation: Still requires human orchestration of steps
Use Case: Answering current-events questions, accessing company documents

Example in Work: - Q: “What time is the last bus?” - LLM: “I don’t know, let me check the bus schedule [tool] → 8:45 PM” - You still coordinate what comes next





Definition: Multiple AI steps connected in sequence; steps are pre-defined
Capability: “Every Monday, summarize feedback → sort by topic → draft report”
Automation Level: Repeats same steps automatically
Limitation: If something unexpected happens, it fails; no adaptation
Use Case: Scheduled, repetitive processes

Example in Work: - Monday morning → AI runs same process → Report auto-generated - BUT: If feedback format changes, process breaks





Definition: LLM + Tools + Memory + Loop that decides its own next steps

WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) gives you a Linux terminal inside Windows. Some part of the courses will be written in commands. The course commands are written for Linux, so this is the one path that works the same for everyone.
Open PowerShell as administrator and run:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Restart when asked, open Ubuntu from the Start menu, and create a username and password.






ImportantKeep projects inside WSL



Work in your Linux home folder (~), not in /mnt/c/... (the Windows drive). Files there are much slower and cause line-ending and permission errors with Git and coding agents. To open a folder in Windows Explorer from the WSL terminal, run explorer.exe ..

5. Store your keys safely
Keys are passwords: anyone who has one can use your quota, and a leaked key can be billed to you.
The default agent, Gemini CLI, uses your Google login and needs no key. The other agents use a free OpenRouter key, which gives access to free models through one account.

Sign up at https://openrouter.ai and create a key. Choose a model marked as free.
Create a file named .env in your project folder and put the key in it:
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-key-here
Never paste the key into code, notebooks, AGENTS.md, screenshots, chat messages or prompts.
Keep .env out of Git (see section 6 for the .gitignore file).







WarningFree tiers can use your prompts



On many free plans the provider may use what you send to improve its models. Do not send private, personal or organisational data to any hosted tool. Use synthetic or public data in exercises. Section 9 gives the full checklist.

text:
6. Folder structure and where files go
Create one workspace folder and keep everything for the series in it:
~/unv-agentic-ai/
├── projects/          # one folder per Git repository you clone or create
│   ├── hello-agent/   # Session 0 deliverable
│   └── ...
├── exercises/         # notes and small experiments
├── data/              # local data files; never committed
└── scratch/           # throwaway tests you can delete at any time
Create it in one step:
mkdir -p ~/unv-agentic-ai/{projects,exercises,data,scratch}
Naming rules: lower-case words joined by hyphens, such as my-first-agent. Avoid spaces and accents. Do not keep projects in a folder synced by OneDrive, Google Drive or Dropbox, because sync tools corrupt the .venv folder and Git history.

Every project starts with a .gitignore file

Then create the repository:
cd ~/unv-agentic-ai/projects
mkdir hello-agent && cd hello-agent
git init -b main


AGENTS.md: tell the agent how to work
AGENTS.md is a plain-text file the agent reads before it changes your code. Put your project rules in it: the language, the test command, the folders it may edit, and what it must never do. This is the project rules file from Session 2. A starter template:
# Project rules

- Language: Python 3.12. Dependencies are managed with uv.
- Run tests with: uv run pytest
- Only edit files inside src/ and tests/.
- Never read or print the contents of .env.
- Ask before deleting any file.
